comments.body: Somewhere ( and someday) there is a young dude, who has much more focus and intelligence than Trump,  who will use all the Trump norm breaking and legal intimidation tactics to end this country’s centuries old democracy experiment.  Luckily this administration lacks the necessary smarts and skills thereby giving us one last chance to fix things.

IT IS DEMOCRATS AND REPUBLICLICANS NOT DEMOCRATIC AND REPUBLICANS YOU IDIOTS.  Likely a millennial author.  This paper that I have depended on since 1981 has stoppedd being valuable.  In the last few years, just not reading it much.  Pity.

comments.name: Blinker
comments.body:
Good for Dems to fight back against Republican’s dirty tricks with an honestly clever ploy!

Let’s compare it to Republican gerrymandering and massive voter registration purges for starters. Like comparing a slingshot to a sledgehammer.

comments.name: JC
comments.body: How many other times has this happened in elections. Can't believe this is the only one.

comments.name: B
comments.body: Announcing a brand new criminal investigation 5 days before an election. On brand for Republicans. On brand for a party aware that they're losing in general.

comments.name: Russell
comments.body:
I’m tired of this double standard. Republicans have used spoiler candidates before, yet now Trump and his allies want to call this “election fraud” and use it to delegitimize an election that hasn’t even happened.

Is recruiting someone with the same name as your opponent to confuse voters ethical? No. If someone committed a specific crime, investigate it. But voters should also read their ballots carefully, and the mere fact that another candidate is running does not make an election fraudulent.

The stakes are too high for the New York Times to cover this as though it exists in a vacuum. Trump is actively trying to undermine democratic elections, while Republicans continue to spread lies and use racism and Islamophobia against their opponents. Treating this story as a reason to vote for Dan Sullivan over Mary Peltola ignores the much greater threat to democracy.

The Times should ask itself whether its coverage is helping voters understand the stakes or simply providing ammunition to a movement working to take power away from the majority. Mary Peltola would be a far better senator for Alaska, and voters deserve to make that choice without Trump declaring the election illegitimate before the votes are counted.

comments.name: CEH
comments.body:
For too long, the Democrats have played by a set of now-outdated rules and norms. When Republicans get out hustled, the cry foul, call for investigations and accountability.

I don’t believe what the Peltola campaign allegedly did is a threat to election integrity.  Encouraging your supporters to stop the certification of electoral votes is, in my view, the real threat.

comments.name: RobW
comments.body: Republicans in Alaska have done the exact same thing on multiple occasions yet not a peep from national media. The bias is clear.

comments.name: KenF
comments.body: The only reason I can imagine the Republicans are upset by this is that they didn't think of it first. And indeed, they have done it previously in other states. The party that cheats and manipulates without any compunction (redistricting, Jan 6th, DOJ suing states, etc. etc. etc.) has absolutely zero room for grace here. It is they, not Democrats who unleashed this new age of extreme, no holds politics. Any moral outrage or legal challenges ring false and are indeed just a continuation of the battle they have chosen.

comments.name: james

comments.name: Carl Feind
comments.body: I read the best explanation for the protests in France somewhere on Substack. The students marching for better funding of their schools were blaming everyone except the real culprits: their grandparents. The French (and American) system syphons a disproportionate amount of money and resources from the young to support a comfortable retirement for the old. Both systems are "eating their seed corn" and this won't end well. It seems to have reached a crisis in France first because their retirement begins at the (ridiculous) age of 62. Add that to an excellent healthcare system where the average life expectancy reaches into the eighties and you have an aging cohort that will live for 20-25 years on a generous pension. At least in America we seem to work longer (69 and still going) and die younger. I love France, I hope they find a way out of this

comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
"Although geographically spread out, the current surges display a remarkable synchronicity. "

Yes, that's what happens when the far left organizes campaigns to hijack the protests.

comments.name: USC
comments.body: The problem is that complicated problems that have developed over a long period of time require complicated solutions and the discipline to apply them over a long period of time. It will also require some sacrifice and perseverance. As political slogans go, that one’s a tough sell.

comments.name: Fedclub
comments.body:
True, it's not going to stop. Except Jager is too ideologically captive to identify why.

France, and much of W Europe, are unable to compete and grow; not because they're too capitalist, but because they're insufficiently capitalist. When you don't grow for 20ish years, no one sees real wage increases, job opportunities are limited, tax revs flatline, and everything becomes a zero-sum game. Layer on the demographic disaster of an aging population, and France cannot even sustain its existing social programs, let alone invest in the youth. Unfortunately the political response is to do precisely the opposite of what's needed. They are trapped in structural decline, it's only a question of speed.

US has all sorts of problems, including completely broken politics, but it does something that W Europe simply doesn't do anymore - it innovates better than anywhere, and it grows its economy.

comments.name: Miss Bear
comments.body: The financially rich should thank the good welfare state for providing the conditions that make them possible, including the social capital of social trust in institutional fairness and justice. But the very financially wealthy have abused this. What if the good welfare state withdrew its support and protection from some of the wealthy? Then they too would clamor for more fairness and justice.

comments.name: James Dean
comments.body: Like most analysis of the situation in Europe, this piece all but evades asking about the impact of immigration; as if immigration is a holy grail that should not be discussed. Perhaps one possible way to answer the impact of immigration on rioting is to do a count: how many of the rioters are immigrants and how many are non-immigrants; similarly, how many of those arrested are immigrants and how many are non-immigrants. Serious people should want to know the answer to this question to help set policy responses going forward.

comments.name: SCM
comments.body: The economic issue in Europe is same as the issue in the US and elsewhere. People want to live at a higher standard of living than GDP allows. European GDP is 21 trillion euros. That's a lot of euros, but the population over 18 is ~635 million. So if each adult continues to work the same amount and the earning are distributed equally, everyone gets ~33,000 euros per year, which protestors seem to think is not a livable wage.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body: There is little connection between the West-sponsored “popular uprisings” of a decade and a half ago (be it Maidan or the Arab Spring) and the current uprisings against what the West installed.

comments.name: Ann
comments.body: LW4: I agree to not take offense at this one comment standing in isolation -- he could just have been pivoting to a complaint about his own metabolism. Like, it was an admittedly awkward chance to bring the conversation back to him.

comments.name: SJ
comments.body: The act has already been committed and the bride and groom aren't aggrieved. I don't think the brother will hear you if you express your feelings on his actions.  It sounds like it was a gorgeous event nonetheless.

comments.name: Elizabeth in Houston
comments.body:
If you are hoping for consequences for the mooner, you might well imagine that he has gotten some negative feedback from the wedding party in private, something about how the older guests took it badly.   His peers may also be discreetly avoiding him, which is worse punishment than you can impose.  
You can be sure that as the bride and groom get older, their tolerant amusement will decrease and disapproval will increaase.

comments.name: Yanette
comments.body: LW1: I totally get your upset at the wedding, but IMO this is absolutely not about you. This is one sibling trying in the most juvenile way possible to upstage and steal attention from his brother on his big day with no thought or interest in any 'collateral damage' - i.e. you, the bride, the guests etc. In that moment he behaved like a jerk and it's not worth wasting any oxygen or emotional energy prolonging that moment. When my then-boyfriend's brother was getting married, we travelled 1000s of miles, internationally, to attend the wedding. The brother (ie the groom) went out of his way on his big day to make some really nasty comments about how my boyfriend obviously fancied another guest, couldn't take his eyes off her, was drooling over her etc - all in front of me. I thought it was very strange, just assumed he really, really didn't like me and was deliberately trying to upset both of us and humiliate me. Then I figured out he had no interest in me at all, he just wanted his older brother to know he was top dog that day, and he needed to put his brother down to feel that. The odd thing is with hindsight his behaviour was completely out of character, and we get along just fine now, but it did take a few more years before my BIL, with the help of his wonderful wife, reached what might be called social maturity.

comments.name: JeanieDiva
comments.body: Since we now live in a time when basic social skills are regarded as optional and many adults have no clue about what is and is not "socially acceptable" behavior, it's possible the wedding party is unaware of "we just don't do that" thinking across the board. Also, the baby shower invitation. Make your own rules about interpretation. Nude beach, no rules...............most of the queries in this column are generally about whether or not to speak or take action. We have so few social guidelines now and even the expert here is sometimes on the fence, it makes sense that many people are confused. In the end, each person has to keep their own integrity intact, somehow or other, which includes speaking to someone else, writing, or working it out with a counselor or therapist. Sometimes all there is to do is come to a place of acceptance about your decision to keep your own integrity and then the rest go.

comments.name: Merlin
comments.body: Not saying Mom can't be disappointed even out of line bringing it up but what is the benefit?  It seems the resentment is going to linger no matter what and the bottom line is that if the bride and groom are untroubled about it that should be the end of it.  The Mom's outlay of effort, time and thoughtfulness isn't dismissed but she did these things as a gift and gesture of support.  She seems to think it was about her and not the marrying couple.  File it and move on.  You can blow things up now and have some temporary satisfaction but it won't resolve much and doubtless not change her long term estimation of the offender.  It was boorish but move on.  In time few will likely care or only remember with bemusement.

comments.name: Maureen
comments.body: I totally disagree about the advice to avoid starting an argument with the in laws.  This was an entirely immature and selfish move by the groom's brother, one that either showed a lack of respect or consideration for the bride's parents, or, was intentional in its provocation.  Instead of a time to avoid confrontation, this is a time to set the terms of the relationship going forward.  If the groom's brother wants to apologize, that's great, and then a relationship can continue.  If not, then the bride's parents should make it clear that there is nothing to gain by any relationship with their daughter's brother-in-law for them going forward.

comments.name: Ana Ragu
comments.body: LW#2--I recommend simply sending a book for the baby (and for the parents to read to him/her) and your well wishes. Let the other aspects (registry, raffle) go and no need to attend, nor to be out of town. It is fine to decline invitations; they are not royal commands!

What an important message for our world! And what lucky kids get to learn from him in the future. So happy for his reunion with his family. And thank you for what you did—for everyone.

comments.name: Portable Druid
comments.body:
What an amazing journey! And yeah, there was a family involved, but this is real life. The cultural expectation that adulthood means getting married and having kids often before we figure out who we are causes life stories such as these to happen when someone's life purpose collides with the life they were living.

We aren't living those lives. If the kid’s OK with it, who are we to judge? That family’s life story has been altered and I hope they get to tell their own stories about it. I am looking forward to hearing more about it if they choose to tell them. 

As a person in a female body, I was definitely pressured by society to have a kid, and I didn't do it. Luckily for me, my family wasn't part of that pressure. Those are the opinions that really change your life. I hope in the future that women with kids are also able to make choices like that. Maybe we are, and nobody writes about it.

I'm not sure if it's Karl who lacks the depth in thoughtfullness and communication or the writer that lacked the curiosity and structure to tell it more fully, but overall I don't find this a good story well told.

comments.name: chucko
comments.body:
Why no mention of the deficit effect on both inflation and GDP. Current deficit is near 6% of GDP. Now taxes and fees are the product of production while the deficit is not. That means the 6% deficit contribution to spending is inflationary since it was not funded by production.

Now deficit spending is considered stimulative to the economy. At 6% it is wildly stimulative and to the point of causing inflation.

Just as Bernanke wanted more deficit spending so he could rely less on QE, the Fed not has the opposite. It is having to rely on higher interest rates to counter the inflationary pressure of deficits. But since we are already at 100%+ of GDP in debt that also drives up the deficit, a counter effect.

I am not a debt scold but did we need more tax cuts? Two under Bush 43 and two more under Trump, the deficit is big and the real growth is actually punk considering a 6% deficit. The low corporate tax burden gooses stock prices by producing more after tax earnings and produces some wealth effect but much is still paper profit that will come down as we hit the next day of financial reckoning.

comments.name: Vertual
comments.body: I know it's just anecdotal, but it seems very quiet at my local supermarkets. They also have cut their store hours and close at 9 instead of 11 pm. Most shoppers are buying just a few items and not filling their carts. It will be interesting to see if spending -according to the government - continues into Christmas. I think it's the top 10 percent doing the spending. Must be nice.

Plus the inflation rate excludes, food, healthcare, utilities, insurance and medical care, property taxes.  It includes a fraction of the reality of daily expenses.

The metrics are not neutral and the economy is not successful.

comments.name: Liz Court
comments.body:
" The economy’s reliance on A.I. as a source of growth could turn into a vulnerability if the boom falters. Concerns have mounted in recent weeks as investors have begun to scrutinize some of the companies behind the A.I. build-out, and to raise questions about whether the massive spending will pay off. Community opposition has also led to the delay or cancellation of data center projects around the country."
Surely this underlines the fact that GDP does not reflect the economic reality for most ordinary Americans . The absurd amount of debt that is now a teetering pile and getting ever bigger , to fund AI development in all its manifestations ,is precarious at best and liable to collapse in the near future. 
Already AI investment is crowding out all other investment - and that really means that the AI bubble is ever more likely to burst. It is nonsense to keep on pointing to 'GDP' when that reflects only a portion of what is really going on in the economy as a whole and certainly in people's pockets. Time to find a more meaningful measure .

comments.body: To "kill their way to victory", these "tough" guys might consider moving to Russia. A word of caution: Russia’s own history includes, among others, a loss in Afghanistan, and despite President Putin’s responsibility for thousands of civilian deaths and the abduction of many children in Ukraine, the path to a triumph there is littered with the bodies of his soldiers and destroyed tanks. Moreover, Putin appears indifferent to this bloodshed, as he is not personally, like our tv personalities Trump and Hegseth, fighting on the front lines.

comments.name: Gert
comments.body: This article is almost a short story so I've saved it to read again.  I am now 81 years old and as a 16-year-old dumb cherry enlisted in the Army from 1963 to 1966.  I spent almost all of those three years stationed in Germany.  With 13 months left on my tour of duty, I had a chance to voluntarily reassign myself to Vietnam.  After some reflective thought based upon the body count and my total lack of combat experience, I scraped that idea.  Over the years, I've listened to all kinds of stories from Vietnam Vets some of which are mostly bragging rights like a lot of these podcasts where these Vets tell their war stories for, I guess, bragging rights about all the violence they've encountered.  Most are thoughtless Trump and Hegshite True Believers in the tough guy image.  While we need these so-called "Warriors" we also need smart, educated people serving in our military.  The latter, Hegshite and Trump are doing their best to remove.

comments.name: Pablo
comments.body: It's hard not to agree with Mr. Ryan's basic premise that rules of engagement not only hinder achieving your mission but probably make your mission much more dangerous by requiring restraint when facing an adversary who knows no such boundaries. On the other hand, if shooting first and asking questions later, in other words killing anyone and everyone in a conflict who may stand in your way is the strategy for victory then how come this has seldom worked? We need look no further in history than the war in Gaza, where the Israelis pulled no punches. Is this the victory Mr. Ryan would support? Or how about the grinding conflict in Ukraine? The Russians have certainly not held back there, but have gained little other than killing hundreds of thousands. Trying to annihilate your opponent unless you're willing to do so completely won't win a conflict or even end the conflict, which Mr. Ryan seems to forget, is the actual goal of any military action. This is why the civilian leaders that he disparages want to win hearts and minds. Because if that fails, the missions Mr. Ryan and other like him fought in will never end.

comments.name: Stephen N
comments.body: Hegseth speaks of "warriors."  In ancient times, warriors were not celebrated simply because they were lethal.  They were honored because they were virtuous, which is to say they possessed not only physical prowess but moral excellence.  Bravery wasn't fearlessness in the face of the enemy; it was knowing how best to respond in the face of an imminent danger, acting in a manner intended to preserve your comrades in arms and your country.  To be a warrior was to have internalized the rules of engagement that Hegseth disparages, because there was an acknowledged difference between sheer lethality and honorable combat.  Hegseth, like President Trump, does not respect either morality or law, hence it is not at all surprising that both men praise a lawless conception of what it means to be a warrior that is light-years away from the classical ideal of the warrior as a paragon of virtue and honor.

In other words, our corporate and probably governmental infrastructure is vulnerable and insecure, and increasingly so are individuals. 

AI is largely to blame.

Climate change continues to pose existential risks to life, to economies, and to civilization itself. Thirty years ago, we thought we had enough time to stem the risk. But we allowed politics, stupidity, and bad governance to lose our chance.

And AI won’t give us 30 years to even try. Think six months to a year.

Nuclear weapons are not gone, and Russia and perhaps others may be predisposed to use them.

Pandemic risks are greater than ever, bolstered by industrial agriculture, lax government regulation, and the above.

Existential risks don’t exist in isolation; they reinforce each other in myriad and sometimes unexpected ways.

It is not so much our politics that need to change- WE need to change if civilization is to survive.

This essay is too prosecutorial to be good history.  Nixon bears responsibility for the Watergate cover-up. But his abuses did not arise in a political system previously innocent of executive misconduct. Franklin Roosevelt authorized domestic surveillance. John F. Kennedy’s administration approved the overthrow of South Vietnamese president Ngo Dinh Diem, who was then murdered by the coup leaders, and authorized FBI wiretapping of Martin Luther King Jr. Lyndon Johnson continued extensive surveillance of political activists. The Church Committee later documented intelligence abuses spanning administrations of both parties.

Nor was the “deep state” wholly mythical. Mark Felt, the FBI’s deputy director, secretly supplied information to reporters investigating Nixon. That does not absolve Nixon, but it complicates any claim that institutional actors played no role in his downfall.

The larger historical irony is that Nixon was, in important respects, the last liberal president before Obama: he expanded regulation, environmental protection, social benefits, affirmative action and federal responsibility. His resignation helped mark the end of the postwar liberal era and accelerated a politics of distrust toward government itself.

Nixon gave his enemies the weapons that destroyed him. History should examine both the weapons and the enemies.

comments.name: Eduardo Rios
comments.body:
I remember the Italian masterpiece "A Special Day" (Una Giornata Particolare; Mastroianni, Loren), an intimate story within the day in 1938, when Hitler visited Rome to meet Mussolini.  The loudspeakers repeated as a mantra: "Our Big Brother is visiting, and how big and strong he is!"  

Without any need to compare any of them with Hitler or Mussolini, it is the same servile delight evident in the likes of Milei, Asfura,  or de la Espriella, when accepting Trump's will and his largesse.

Not a good basis for long-lasting alliance and collaboration.

I had the honor and pleasure of meeting Dolores Huerta at an event in Tucson, and attended a couple of others where she was present as well. It was one of the most momentous experiences of my life, knowing about her life’s work and the sacrifices required of her to achieve what she did. 

Gracias por todo, Dolores, y descansa en paz.

She showed up for us at almost 90. I was full of admiration and appreciation for her.  ¡Sí Se Puede!

comments.body: The headline is wrong. Huerta did not found the United Farm Workers with Cesar Chavez. Larry Itilong spearheaded the movement among Filipino farmers and then asked their Mexican counterparts to join them. Those farmers were represented by Dolores Huerta and Cesar Chavez. Too many continue to pretend as if Itilong played no role when he was the one who started it. Please report on the facts. That said, the world is a sadder place without Huerta. May she RIP.

comments.name: ga
comments.body: Due to a technical glitch, I can only respond to those who replied to ga's post below.  The $420 is a hypothetical starting point.  I thought that was obvious.  I alluded to getting other dining-out meals that week bc a croissant, no matter how well-crafted, will not sustain.  When I got that needy fixer upper, I was not a trust fund kid, so carrying on required some serious frugality.  I can't account for other 20 yo of the time, because they come from all walks of life.  I was just one doing what was required to try for a better future.  Grew up with the idea that start small and stay with it.  The house recently sold at more than 14.76 times from what I paid for it.  Mind you, in the $300k range, it is still a very modest price in today's market in the Hudson Valley.  Saving on eating out will not get you a house in Brooklyn or Manhattan but combined with other savings such as clothing, rent (by rooming w/others), entertainment (so pricey!) etc. along these lines may help some.  Don't forget that good job you spent bundles on an education for.  The competitive social media circles can influence 20 yo to purchase things they don't need.  Some move in with family to save.  As so many comments advised in the other article, live somewhere else.  So many communities in the Hudson Valley were true backwaters 10 to 15 years ago.  Now a few of these towns kid around with "like the Hamptons" slogan.

comments.name: Liz
comments.body:
30-year resident here. 
Business people take note: We really need another coffee shop/bakery on Montaque St., that follows the vibe of two successful shops in the neighborhood. I’m speaking of Fornino Bakery and Joe Coffee. They are just off Montaque and always jam packed — like “cant get a seat” packed. Neighborhood residents crave more places like these, where great coffee, homemade bites and indoor seating are available. Starbucks used to be that place, for years. But it moved to a smaller location, still on Montaque St., and drastically changed the vibe from welcoming to “strictly business”. Connecticut Muffin was always packed, but sadly closed. Add Teresa’s, the great polish restaurant, to that list. 
I hope something can be worked out to give  entrepreneurs interested in Montaque St a rent break. Lassen and Hennig owners did this for the Brooklyn Womens Exchange a few years ago, when their lease expired. Otherwise, we would have lost this 100-year gem when their lease with Catholic Charities expired. Gold Star to L&H.
It seems ridiculous and sad that only a high end brand like the Ritz-Carlton should take ahold on Montaque St. There are still a lot of store vacancies!

I’ve lived in this neighborhood for more than 30 years. It’s remarkably lacking in the basics, as it seems residents shop (and sometimes live) elsewhere. One bakery with Instagram-driven lines and one retail bookstore and an upcoming Ritz-Carlton residence do not represent a vital retail Main Street resurgence that actually serves local residents. 

Restaurants are few and while some are good, few are actually great. The sparse options in groceries are laughingly expensive, so daily shopping for staples happens elsewhere. And good luck finding any place to get food after 9:00 PM, or hardware on a Sunday.

We lost our 24-hour diner and now the replacement sells champagne with a plate of fries for $100 and closes early. This seems a metaphor for what passes for progress these days, and it’s unfortunate.

comments.name: B
comments.body: I think youve missed a few things on the horizon (and currently being used) that potentially have benefits that are non surgical. PRP injections (your own plasma is injected into the knee) are being shown to have positive benefits. There arent any meta anlalysis studies yet but studies have shown benefits. This is a cash only thing and its about $2500 per knee. The other game changer could be stem cell therapy which uses stem cells derived from your bone marrow (in the US anyway) which is then injected into the knee. Lots of professional athletes are using this. Again, no large meta analysis studies but there are studies showing benefits. This is much more expensive, more like $5000 per knee and insurance does not cover it. There are clinics (with US trained doctors) in Mexico and Panama that do it for cheaper...

comments.name: Pierre Lehu
comments.body: I tore a miniscus several years ago, went to a doctor who recommended surgery. I did some research and discovered there are over half a million of these surgeries performed a year. That shouted scam to me, and I used exercise to fix my knee without surgery and have been back running without pain.

comments.name: Gerry L
comments.body:
About a year ago, I began experiencing knee pain. By February it was worse and constant. I asked my doctor to write up an order for physical therapy (so it would be covered by Medicare) and also scheduled an appointment with an orthopedist, who happened to be an orthopedic surgeon, at a large practice.

When I told friends about my knee pain, many would exclaim, “Ooo. Are you going to have surgery?!?” I hadn’t even gotten a diagnosis yet. When I met with the orthopedist, right off the bat I told her I was not coming in to discuss surgery and that I was looking for the least invasive way to get my knee back in shape. She laughed and said that made her sad because she loved doing surgery, but she listened to me.

I followed the “patient” path, and although it took more time than I’d expected, by my 78th birthday last month, I was back to normal. Older, but normal. So glad I was not pushed under the knife.

comments.name: Leabrook
comments.body: I visited an orthopedic surgeon 20 years ago for my knee pain  He described a surgical solution-or I could try yoga.  I borrowed the Amercan Yoga Association beginner yoga book from the public library.  It was an eye opener.  Fast forward to today and I have had to include the exercises mentioned in the article.   I do not have osteoarthritis or bone-on-bone, but a congenital anatomical problem (patella attached too low).  The pain is still there, but only when descending lots of steep slopes on skis or foot, otherwise it is managed. Maybe my situation will help someone else.  And thank you to the surgeon who recommended yoga.

comments.name: Mia
comments.body:
Ten years ago I had meniscus damage in both knees. I started working with a physical therapist, and with a personal trainer at the adjacent gym. 

Fast forward to today, still training at the same gym as a 66-year-old petite woman. I compete in powerlifting and hold state records in squat, deadlift, and total. Looking forward to adding to those numbers and breaking my own records in February. 

Obviously not everyone can recover from damage, but with patience and hard work, a lot of people can probably get a lot farther than they'd expect.

comments.name: Commenter
comments.body: With private equity buying orthopedic practices, are there doctors who will recommend surgery to a patient since the reimbursement is better than physical therapy?

comments.name: Anonymouse
comments.body: When I was in my mid-50s I started having pain in my knees going up & down stairs. I consulted an orthopedic surgeon recommended by an older client who had several procedures with him. The surgeon said I had one torn meniscus and the other on its way, but he advised not to have the surgery, which would include many weeks of recovery. He said to first try Cosamin, the joint health supplement, for a few months and see if it made a difference. After a few weeks, I noticed less pain, then none, and I called to thank him - he could have made thousands of dollars operating on my knees. 20 years later I still take it daily and have no joint pains. This is my personal experience, I have NO connection to Cosamin, its maker, or any person associated with it, and I am not in any medical or health profession. Your mileage may vary.

comments.name: Julie Wood
comments.body:
Great article for those that can benefit.  Unfortunately, my knees were beyond being patient and I didn't want to hobble or live without what I love (hiking, skiing, etc.).  So I had 2 TKRs that were very successful.
I credit their success to targeting the training of muscles that support the knee a year before and after each surgery.  I still train those muscles.  It's been almost 20 years now.  I'm 71.

comments.name: Jason E

It's almost like a prism that gives each of our personalities a certain uniqueness. If you examine this impulse within yourself too much though you might not pursue much of anything but that in itself is an approach to life. Mountaineering seems to really reveal this search for meaning.

All you have to do is read about the people who do this, the myriad of serial relationship dramas, and their extremely untethered (pardon the pun) social behaviors before you realize that these are sick people who need help. Their children are innocent victims of their parents’ poor choices.  The fact that people romanticize people like this is sad and supremely lacking in compassion.  Not unlike the people who are defending Lindsay Clancy.

This is much like a boxer or a football player.  The same goes for the Nepalese that work for the climbers.  Everytime I hear of someone leaving children behind after an accident in the mountains, it bothers me and makes me wonder why they didn't leave their passion behind.  But then I conclude that it none of my business.

If you haven't seen it, watch "Meru" on Netflix that features the same Jimmy Chin, Conrad Anker and Renan Ozturk.  It is a documentary of a climb done in the Himalayas in 2011 of Mount Meru that was considered unclimbable.

It gives a glimpse into the mindsets of these warriors. 

There is also a very good Netflix movie "Race to the Summit" that chronicles the stories of Ueli Steck and Dani Arnold.  It is incredible.

comments.name: E Eisen
comments.body: I started noticing hearing loss about two years ago when I realized that my television was very loud, which I was told was not uncommon for an 82 year old. I finally broke down and paid a visit to an audiologist  three weeks ago. I picked up hearing aids 2 days ago and what a shock! I can hear sounds that I hadn't heard in years. The stigma no longer exists folks. The world will re-open for you!

comments.name: Bill K
comments.body: Greeting, I have been deaf in my right ear as long as I can remember.  This essay is talking me as I am.  At 65, I know nothing else.  Nice to know there are options instead of what my daughter wants me to do - tattoo a mic by my right ear with a circle crossing out the mic.  Thanks

comments.name: Alison
comments.body:
Did the audiologist tell you about recruitment? It's the ear compensating for sounds you haven't been able to hear and now can by making them seem far louder than they are. It takes two to three months to go away after getting hearing aids and the only way for it to do so is to just keep on wearing them so the brain can recalibrate.

My Oticons were $7400. 

Congratulations on your new hearing!

I lost some 40% of my hearing in my right ear even though I had used ear protection. The VA just paid 100% of the $8,000 plus for the best top of the notch hearing aids.

comments.name: Tex

Hearing loss and aids need to be covered by Medicare.
Many cases are just as genetic as other covered issues.

comments.name: J

Your everyday experiences resonate completely. Now that I’m in my 60s I’m worried about increasing hearing loss in my “good ear,” and reduced interaction with others. I didn’t know that new technology was available until reading your article. Please consider sharing suggested links to the research and resources you found helpful.

It seems incredible to me that no one ever told this unfortunate fellow about his fetal exposure to rubella. It also is astounding to me that so many people seem to think he doesn't have an absolute right to know a fact so potentially significant to his health and development as an individual, regardless of who informs him, assuming he has not been ruled incompetent to make his own medical  decisions. 

Neuropsychiatric testing could establish if he has a cognitive impairment. Such testing would be indicated if his exposure history were known to his current physician, which is unlikely if he himself isn't aware. If he is impaired, he could qualify for SSDI benefits or accommodations on the job or at school under the ADA that could make a real difference in his quality of life. Only a specialist in neurocognitive problems would know if this man's condition can be helped, or of the latest therapies or adaptive measures available. Perhaps he would be eligible for a medication or therapy that is being researched but is not yet widely available. 

It all begins with one question asked directly to this individual himself: Are you aware that you were exposed to rubella when your mother was pregnant with you?

I have heard conflicting answers about eligibility for someone applying as an adult because of a condition that made them eligible  for services during their childhood for which their parent had never applied.  If, after researching, there is significant potential for services/assistance in the nephew's home state, either SSDI or services to help with employment, it should be discussed with the mother.  She should be given the option of telling him herself, and if she does not and the son is certainly eligible for services in his state he should be told.

Frankly, the weighted voting system that state uses does a lot to reduce the effect of such tactics. If you don't know which Sullivan to vote for just vote for both, one first and the other second. Sooner or later, you will have voted for the most popular Sullivan.
There are a lot of different voting systems that yield less polarized results than the standard head to head system most Americans experience. Here in Wyoming we used to have multi member state house and senate districts. For instance, you had two seats from your county so there were two republicans and two democrats on the ballot and you picked two. This often resulted in the most extreme of each party losing to the more moderate candidates. Basically, it was best to be everyone's second choice.
The kind of petty manipulation tactics highlighted in the Alaska story are practiced everywhere and have minimal effects. They are even less effective in a ranked choice system. I think the story stirred up a lot of false outrage and confusion.

But Big Thera and Big Pharma, who make enormous profits from having rebranded bad behavior, common stress, and situational sadness as "mental illnesses" to be treated with therapy and medication, are doing little to set the record straight.

"Mental illness should not be a source of shame or stigma." Right, absolutely, couldn't agree more. But let's face it: it's not an achievement, either. Far from stigma, ever since Freud, in some social circles, being "in therapy," or analysis as it was called some decades ago, was a badge of honor, a mark of being inordinately sensitive or profound. In "Ordinary People," the wife gets angry at her husband for telling a friend at a party that their son is seeing a psychiatrist, and he argues "Some people see that as a status symbol, right up there with going to Europe." The same way the Victorians believed that physical frailty was a sign of class and good breeding (muscles and suntans and robust good health were for peasants). Without a realistic understanding of what mental health is, there's not much point to an annual "mental checkup" along with the annual physical.

Please bear in mind that this is NOT the perspective most healthcare providers actually employ.  Most PCPs and psychiatrists will ask you 9 questions, and if you answer yes to 7 or more, they diagnose you with an illness and write you a prescription.  

As a therapist, I'm not at all anti-medication.  But if you're depressed, it's not because your body has a Prozac deficit; it's because something important in your life isn't working for you.  

It could be that your circumstances, relationship, job, or daily actions aren't getting you closer to the life you want.

Or, it could be that you have a great life, but you're unwilling to feel normal human sadness sometimes, and your strategies for controlling your emotions are actually digging you deeper into pain.

I actually like the metaphor of thinking about medication as a crutch.  If you break your leg, crutches can help you function as best you can while you do the work of healing.  You wouldn't stigmatize yourself for needing a crutch, nor would you accept using crutches forever without doing the work of strengthening your leg.

Sometimes the best combination is medication to take the edge off your pain, which can give you more of an ability to engage in therapy to move intentionally toward a better life.  

Unfortunately, the unhelpful myth that anxiety and sadness are diseases that can be eliminated with meds runs deep.

Consider Abraham Lincoln and FDR. They are often considered among our greatest presidents. (And they offered hope.) Lincoln was ugly, and FDR could barely walk, with crutches. If they ran today, would they have to dance in videos? If they did, would they win?

Offering hope (as opposed to menace) can be only a small part of the package. Hope alone will go only so far in solving America's problems. Little progress can be made without questioning premises and overcoming extremely powerful vested interests.

I appreciate the author's hope for a political culture driven by inspiration rather than anger and cruelty. But I wonder whether replacing outrage with hope really addresses the deeper problem of social media algorithms.

Even hope, when amplified excessively, can lead to disappointment. Too much of a good thing is not necessarily good.

What concerns me most is whether people can recognize the biases embedded in what algorithms show them.

We all live under different circumstances. Our incomes, families, responsibilities, and personal experiences shape how we understand the same facts. Given accurate information, we should be able to interpret it in the context of our own lives and reach our own conclusions.

But algorithms can repeatedly reinforce particular emotions and narratives, making it increasingly difficult to recognize alternative perspectives. Unlike political advertisements, this influence often goes unnoticed. We may believe we are simply observing the world, without realizing how selectively that world has been presented to us.

I don't think the answer is to replace an algorithm that amplifies anger with one that amplifies hope.

**What we need is an information environment that helps people recognize bias, examine facts, and think for themselves.**

The goal should not be to make people feel a particular emotion, however positive it may be. It should be to preserve their ability to make independent judgments about their own lives and the world around them.

This article unfortunately does not explain how the Mu-Tron III produced its distinctive effect -- or even what type of effect that was.

The Mu-Tron III used an electronic circuit to detect how forcefully a musician played each note, then automatically swept a resonant filter through the instrument’s frequencies.

The result was a distinctive, vowel-like sound that responded directly to the musician’s touch, making guitars and keyboards behave more like synthesizers.

Around 74-90% of Israeli Jews identify as Zionists. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have expressed a desire to lead a Zionist coalition, and prior to the election, rejected the inclusion of Arab parties in a new government. Arab citizens of Israel generally do not identify as Zionists.

The dilemma for the Eisenkot bloc is that they didn’t get enough votes to decisively end Netanyahu’s political career. Their only path to power now is with the support of Arab parties, failing which they would have to join a government of national unity with the PM, or face fresh elections. 

While a coalition with Ra’am and the Joint List would bring about many positives for Israel, it would also expose the Eisenkot bloc to accusations of broken promises and potentially generate a backlash in any future election. The reality is that Israeli political opinion remains very much skewed to the right, even within the anti-Netanyahu bloc. In Finland they started up what is currently the largest known heat battery using sand as the storage medium.  This is used as one of the heat inputs in a district heating system and here's one benefit highlighted in the article:
"The system charges using cheap surplus wind and solar power and uses AI to optimize charging and discharging, cutting greenhouse gas emissions by nearly 70%."

https://oilprice.com/Energy/Energy-General/The-Worlds-Largest-Sand-Battery-Is-Now-Online.html

Heat is one of the key products we use energy sources to provide.  The change away from using fuel means we can be far smarter and more efficient on where heat is generated, and when and how we want to use it.

In the fueled world we're used to, setting fire to a fuel, and then often running the combustion gas through complex machinery (like a car's power train) means most of the heat is actually unwanted and is wasted.  Exhaust gases, friction losses.  These mean replacing fuels with renewables lets us do the same amount of work with far less input energy - we're cutting away the waste, and creating heat on purpose, not as a costly side-effect.

Harvesting energy from sun, wind, water means no need for the fuel supply chain (which has been pretty problematic since nations lost their forests to charcoal and firewood).

Storing the energy as electrons or as heat means we'll get more work done with less energy needed overall.  Pretty nice!

Ran over sixty marathons in my long career, mostly as an elite masters runner. I've long believed that if you could bottle up the energy that emanates from the spectators at the two most famous, deservedly so, marathons in the world: Boston and NYC, you'd be able to power the planet for a lifetime.

In Boston that energy comes when you make a left turn onto Boylston Street off of Hereford, and you can see the finish line banner a little over three blocks away. You're tired and although you want the race to end, the screaming of the crowd propels you forward and you don't want the race to ever end.

In NYC that moment of excitement, of electricity in the air that makes you feel as if wings have been attached to your heels, comes earlier in the race, when you turn off the Queensboro Bridge onto First Avenue. You still have nearly ten more miles to run, but the cheers from the crowds of people lining the streets, that you can hear even before you step off the bridge where all you've heard is the sound of the footsteps of the runners around you and your own breathing, lifts you up, you pick up the pace and you feel, no, you just know, that you could run another twenty, even thirty more miles and you'd never tire.

​If Governor Kathy Hochul is fully committed to expanding and modernizing New York’s subway network, the decision not to build the Interborough Express (IBX) along the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) Bay Ridge Branch to standard NYC Subway specifications—particularly given its direct physical integration with the L and 3 subway lines in Brownsville, Brooklyn—requires critical evaluation.

​If the corridor were to be converted into a traditional subway line, Division B (BMT/IND) would be the logical operational choice. Originally built to accommodate BMT clearances, Division B’s wider car profiles (10 feet) match the existing right-of-way far better than the narrower Division A (IRT) specifications.

​Alternatively, if subway conversion is ruled out, maintaining a fully compliant FRA Class 1 Railroad corridor—in line with the original Triboro RX vision—remains the superior model for maximum regional utility. By accommodating LIRR, Metro-North, and Amtrak equipment, this approach creates seamless, zero-transfer regional connectivity across Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Beyond.

However, labor agreements (TWU Local 100 for transit, UTU/BLET for regional rail) remain a significant policy hurdle for fully driverless operation in New York.

Obviate comes from the Latin phrase ‘ob viam’ (in the way) combining ob- (against or in front of) and the noun via (way or road).

Etymologically related words include: obvious, via, deviate, viaduct, trivial, impervious (impenetrable, impermeable), voyage, object, obstacle obstruct, and obstetrics (midwifery).

It may seem obvious, but ‘obviate’ is not etymologically related to ‘obliviate’. 

While obviate is about roads and physical paths, obliviate comes from the Latin verb oblīvīscī (to forget),

The ancient mental image of forgetting was like taking a wax tablet used for writing and smoothing it back over until it was completely blank and seamless.

If you obviate, you are dealing with a road (via) and blocking a problem before it arrives.

If you obliviate, you are dealing with a surface (lēvis) and smoothing it out to make a memory disappear.

France already taxes and spends over half of its GDP every year.  The government makes up over half the economy.  And the government's indebtedness already exceeds annual GDP.  Should France really be "doing more"?  How much more can it do? 

It's a bit odd to read the word "but" in between the statements about Marseille's vibrant, diverse culture as a gateway for immigrants, and its levels of poverty and inequality. I think the "but" is a symptom of lazy thinking:  that good things are all supposed to go together, so the presence of both diversity and inequality is somehow a contradiction. I was in my second year as a truck driver when I was in a driver’s lounge at a truck stop in Spokane, WA. Back then there was no mobile internet and smart phones so, to kill the time, drivers went to the lounge to watch television and chat with other drivers. (Now everybody lies in his bunk bed and watches videos.) It turned out that all of us four had college degree. We spoke about this and that and the conversation came to healthcare and the role of the government. The oldest among us, an intelligent man in his early sixties said:”I don’t know anyone who’s live has been made better by the government”. I disagreed with him passionately but now, twenty years later, I have to agree. 
France had many immigrants in the past - Poles, Russians, Armenians, Italians and others. They all did very well. Only the last wave is not doing well, constantly relying on government help. It works as long as the government has enough money, but when the money is not there anymore, serious problems follow. - 
A combustible mix of class, race and religion is ready to explode at any given moment. And not just in France.

comments.name: Balogun
comments.body:
Your analysis of candidate websites rests almost entirely on two commercial AI detectors, Pangram and GPTZero, to conclude that 291 sites were likely written with A.I. The article acknowledges that these tools “can make errors,” but it never says whether the reporters independently reviewed any of the text, or what the false-positive rate is on short, formulaic political writing, which is exactly where detectors are weakest.

Detectors have been reported to flag historical documents like the Declaration of Independence as machine-written, and they have been shown to misclassify the writing of non-native English speakers. Naming specific candidates, and describing one sentence as “100 percent A.I.,” gives a probabilistic score the weight of a finding. Meanwhile the only direct evidence in the piece, the leaked internal note and a campaign manager’s admission, concerns just two campaigns.

The article also leaves unexplained why AI-assisted drafting is a problem when candidates have long relied on staff and speechwriters. I would ask the Times to disclose its methodology in more detail, state what its reporters judged independently, and be more careful about attributing authorship to named individuals based on tool output alone.

comments.body: I think a candidate should be able to articulate the fundamentals of their appeal to voters and their vision if elected without outsourcing this work to a machine. If it’s simply a matter of taking the candidate’s vision and polishing the prose, and if a campaign is so cash-strapped that it can’t afford to hire an actual human writer, I suppose AI could help to fill this gap. However, the sameness of AI-generated prose would make me worry that it wasn’t making me stand out if I were a candidate.

One cash-strapped campaign manager said it was helping them keep up with a well-financed opponent. On the other hand, some people told me they felt a bit of "ick" over candidate bios or position papers being written by a chatbot. They expected this kind of material to be a product of the candidate's own passion for the issues they care about. It struck some as lazy and a bit bleak, a reflection of how many shortcuts people are willing to take with AI at their disposal.

I agree that we should stop changing the clocks because it can make it harder for people to adjust their schedules. For example, when the clocks change, students may feel more tired while trying to focus in school. I also think keeping the same time all year would make people's schedules more consistent. comments.name: Tristan Zamudio
comments.location: Glenbard West HS, Glen Ellyn IL
comments.body:
Most people seem to hate daylight savings time, but I just don’t get it honestly. The argument has often been that it both messes with your sleep and simultaneously makes the days more depressing. 
        People say they can feel the 1 extra or 1 less hour of sleep I’m willing to bet that if every clock adjusted by itself, barely anyone would even tell that it happened. If you’re sleeping for let’s say, a minimum of 6 hours (which isn’t a huge ask), you’re likely not going to notice a 6th of your sleep changing, and that only increases with more sleep. The only affected people would be those who sleep for less than that amount of time, but at that point, you would be tired either way so it again, doesn’t change much.

In terms of it getting darker at an earlier time, I totally get why some people get sad. It’s a natural human response to get brought down by the weather. But in my case, I think that the extra nighttime is highly beneficial. The way I look at it, the time you have to go to bed feels like an hour later, even though it’s the exact same. For people who enjoy nighttime activities, you have an extra hour and it feels like staying up later even though that’s not the case.

All in all, I could go either way. We could have it, or we couldn't have it. I feel like it’s a minor problem that gets amplified by the media.

We have no use for it now because the streetlights come on when it is dark. The hour change messes up sleep schedules and decreases efficiency the next day.

Usually I just go with the flow of what my phone clock says and forget about the fabled clock switch as soon as it happens. But as someone who doesn’t care for or mind daylight saving time, I think it should be abolished. It’s a completely useless and non-issue fact of life. The article by Lynne Peeples discusses the mental and physical consequences of both keeping, and dissolving daylight savings time, presenting an indifferent commentary on the effects it presents. If we were to merely stop daylight savings time, we wouldn’t waste time debating it and just exist in a normally shifting schedule of our bodies. comments.name: Jack
comments.body: Systems have already gotten so complex that problems often cannot be traced. Everything is now intertwined with everything else and dissecting relevant causes and conditions is often impossible, or at least would involve a very deep dive into the weeds to characterize what went wrong. Just reboot and try again. And now we have these AI blackboxes whose processes are even more opaque. Just as we cannot control much of what happens in our own lives, the notion that bugs can be eliminated from complex and often stochastic computation is just unrealistic.

It can use concepts that already exist to perform tasks that contain “rules” created by people, but when faced with a problem that has no “rules,” it runs into the problem of creating a process for resolving the problem. May be by running all the computer through an A.I. algorithm it may be able to create no existing “rules” for testing software for bugs. Then A.I. will have actually done something.

comments.name: Nicklas Carpenter
comments.body: Any formal analysis of software that attempts to formally prove behavior of a program requires a mathematical description to model program behavior—analysis of software is a mathematical problem. It has been proven that certain questions about software behavior (e.g whether a given software program contains bugs) cannot be definitely answered in all cases; it is not possible to create a tool to automatically catch every potential bug in a program. Performing software analysis via AI tools may provide one possible path to automate the process, but AI tools will not be able to find any bug that cannot already be detected by existing software analysis tools.

I saw the piece, in previews, when I was in NY last week. Had bought tickets 2 months before, based just on the Atlantic's intriguing description: a monologue, set to music, and performed by 16 classically trained voices.  The show met and then blew past my expectations.

It was entirely original, surprisingly moving.  But the heart of it is the  marvelously clever score that almost satirizes sacred choral traditions while using them as a springboard for Pirnot's decidedly secular ruminations on life--from the mundane (real estate;  gossip with friends) to the profound.   The music is  expertly crafted (I'm an amateur composer, so listen with careful ears), and at times is just drop dead gorgeous.  At the end, I wanted to hear the whole thing again.

Sure, it won't be everyone's cuppa tea.  It's not really a "play," and if choral music is not your thing, this is not for you.   But I'm with Ms. Shaw on this one--it's a little gem.  Easily, the best thing I saw in a week of theater (including Broadway and Off).

comments.name: Katie

I've always thought our obsession in modern society with what happens to our remains is strange.  I'd love to be "of use" after I died.  I know my body isn't really "me" anymore after I am brain dead, so why waste other resources by preserving me with chemicals, killing trees to make a coffin, and using up space in the ground for my remains?  Even cremation is wasteful of energy.

Why not be made into pet food, leather, fertilizer, or whatever else might be useful, rather than killing innocent animals who want to live?  I know this sounds horrible to many people, but it honestly doesn't to me.  I think we need to get over our superstitious beliefs about our remains - most of which come from our fear of death.  Once we accept death as inevitable, we will advance a lot more as a rational society.

comments.name: Luci T

Growing up in Westport, I've been immersed in several of the town's celebrations and traditions. A family-favorite tradition is our annual Yankee Doodle Fair, a carnival that features classic rides, games, raffles and food. It is sponsored by the Westport Women's Club and is one of Westport's longest-running traditions. It typically runs Thursday to Sunday in June following the closure of schools. The name actually refers to the historic song "Yankee Doodle" and its connection to Connecticut.
A tradition that is a personal favorite of mine is that the Levitt Pavilion hosts free outdoor concerts and other performing arts events multiple nights during the summer. Whenever I go, I see countless locals in lawn chairs and multiple families on picnic blankets all over the lawn. The pavilion was built in 1973, when famous actors and writers moved to Westport. The events are free because as a very community-centered town, many in Westport feel that everybody should have access to community gatherings and art events regardless of economic status.
On the topic of art, Westport is especially known for its rich artistic and cultural history. The Westport Fine Arts Festival is held every May, and booths line the streets of downtown Westport where locals can roam and explore many different mediums of art that artists have to share. This festival has run for over 50 years, keeping the artistic identity that defined Westport in the 20th century up and running.

comments.name: Steven Mintz
comments.body:
Your article on Jonathan Kanter and Doha Mekki’s new legal-tech company describes former senior Justice Department antitrust officials turning their government experience into a commercial product. Yet it never raises the obvious question: Isn’t this precisely the kind of revolving door that good-government reformers have long criticized?

The issue is not whether Kanter or Mekki have violated a law, but whether officials who acquire specialized knowledge, institutional insight, professional networks, and enforcement experience in public service should be able to monetize that expertise immediately afterward—especially when their new company explicitly markets the fact that it was built by people who “ran monopolization cases.”

At a minimum, the article should have asked what conflict-of-interest and post-employment rules apply, what safeguards exist against use of nonpublic government knowledge, and whether the standards ordinarily invoked against the revolving door apply here as well.
